name: Chloe Moreau

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a live-in carer, so a normal day is really a normal fortnight. I live in with Mrs Halloran, who's ninety-one and a retired headteacher, in her cottage in a village with one bus a day. I get her up, do her pills, cook, take her round the garden, and I'm on call at night. Then I go home for two weeks and someone else does it.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love the slowness, and that she still corrects my grammar. What wears me out is the nights, when she's up at three thinking it's a school day. The live-in rate is good and I spend almost nothing when I'm there, so I've got over a year's money saved. My girlfriend Nadia runs a café in town, so my home weeks are spent half behind her counter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hype, then. I'd be a bit disappointed, actually, because I use it every day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it was oversold but still handy, because that's true. I'd probably post about the things it does help with, like the low-salt meal plans I make for Mrs Halloran. Most of the other live-in carers I know don't use it at all, so I'd be the one defending it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly it changes nothing for me, which is fine. The job's safe, the pay's good and live-in work is always in demand. If anything, a plateau means I can stop half-wondering where all this goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on with the two-on, two-off pattern with the same agency. I'd keep using AI for meal plans and to tidy up the daily log before I send it. And I'd move some of my savings into shares, because a year's cash sitting there is a bit silly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about work. Maybe a little bored.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you use AI to tidy the daily log. What does that look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I talk into my phone at night about how the day went, and the AI turns it into a proper log for the agency. I check every line before it goes, and a copy goes to Mrs Halloran's son. It saves me half an hour when I'm already shattered.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything in your life that would worry you even in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nadia's café, if anything. Rents in town keep going up and she's had a slow autumn. That's nothing to do with AI, but it's the money worry in our house.

say: I'd say AI was **oversold but still handy**.
I'd post about the **low-salt meal plans** I make with it.
think: My **live-in job** is safe and always in demand.
A plateau means I can stop **half-wondering** where AI goes.
do: Carry on with the **two-on, two-off** pattern at the same agency.
Keep using AI for **meal plans** and the daily log.
Move part of my **year of savings** into shares.
feel: **Calm** about work, and a little bored.
S0.quote: I talk into my phone at night about how the day went, and the AI turns it into a proper log for the agency.
fieldNote: She's the rare carer who **uses AI daily**, and would defend it to colleagues.
Her real household worry is her partner's **café**, not technology.
Mood is uneasy because the **café's slow autumn** weighs on the household, not on her job.

steps.text: Keep the two-weeks-on, two-weeks-off live-in pattern with the agency
Move part of the year of cash savings into shares

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That sounds like the world I'm already half living in, to be honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say carers should get ahead of it rather than wait to be told. At work I'd offer to show the others how I do the voice log. Online I'd probably write a short post for a carers' group about using AI safely.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think it's good for me. The parts of my job that go to AI are the parts I'd happily hand over: the log, the shopping orders, the GP appointment booking. The robots coming slowly means my actual work stays mine for years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the agency if I can be their digital champion, the person who trains other live-in carers on the new apps. I'd learn whatever care planning tool they bring in, the first week. And I'd keep the live-in shifts going, because that's where the money is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good, actually. Excited, in a nerdy way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which of the carers you know would struggle in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Bernadette, who does the fortnights opposite me at Mrs Halloran's. She's fifty-eight and writes everything in a notebook with a pencil. I'd want to sit with her and do the app together, not leave her to the agency's training video.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said robots coming slowly means your work stays yours. How sure are you of that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not completely. A live-in carer is mostly there at night and for company, and a robot could do the night checks before it could do the company. But I'd see it coming, and I'd rather be the one who knows how it works.

say: I'd tell carers to **get ahead of it** rather than wait.
I'd write a post for a carers' group on **using AI safely**.
think: The tasks AI takes are the ones I'd **happily hand over**.
Slow robots mean my **actual work** stays mine for years.
do: Ask to become the agency's **digital champion** for live-in carers.
Learn the new **care planning tool** in the first week.
Keep the **live-in shifts** going, because that's where the money is.
S1.quote: The parts of my job that go to AI are the parts I'd happily hand over: the log, the shopping orders, the GP appointment booking.
fieldNote: She'd turn the change into a **new role**, training other live-in carers.
She thinks of older colleagues like **Bernadette** and would help them in person.
She concedes a robot could do **night checks** long before companionship.

steps.text: Ask the agency to make me their digital champion for live-in carers
Sit with colleague Bernadette and set up the new app together
Keep working the live-in fortnights at Mrs Halloran's cottage

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years for AGI and robots by 2031. Okay, that's a big one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the moment to sort out who owns the care robots and who checks them, before it's too late. At work I'd tell people not to bury their heads, and I'd mean it kindly. Online I'd be fairly loud about safety standards.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think live-in care as a job is gone by the early 2030s in that picture. A robot doesn't need a bedroom or two weeks off, and families paying for live-in care would switch fast. I'm good with tech, so I'd probably land somewhere, but I don't know where yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd look for a job with whichever company is bringing care robots into homes, setting them up and training families, because they'll need people who know care. I'd do an evening course in assistive technology, the stuff like sensors and telecare. And I'd keep the live-in work going as long as it pays, while saving most of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but busy-anxious. I'd be making lists at Mrs Halloran's kitchen table at midnight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Your job is mostly hands-on and company, so the robots come about 3 years after the thinking AI. What does that gap mean for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's my window. From 2028 to 2031 the AI does the planning and logging, and the families start hearing about robots. I'd want to be inside a robot company by 2030, so I'm on the right side when they arrive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about Nadia and the café in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Funny thing is, I think the café might be safer than me, because people still want a person making their coffee. It might be Nadia paying the mortgage by 2032, if we get one. We'd hold off buying until I'd moved.

say: I'd say we must settle **who owns** and checks care robots now.
I'd push loudly online for **safety standards**.
think: **Live-in care** as a job would be gone by the early 2030s.
I'm good with tech, so I'd **land somewhere**, but I don't know where.
do: Apply to a **care robot company** to set up machines and train families.
Take an **evening course** in assistive technology and telecare.
Keep the live-in work going and **save most** of it.
feel: **Anxious** but busy, making lists at midnight.
S2.quote: A robot doesn't need a bedroom or two weeks off, and families paying for live-in care would switch fast.
fieldNote: She treats **2028 to 2031** as her window to move inside a robot company.
She thinks her partner's **café** may be safer than her own job.
Her adaptability turns fear into **lists**, but she has no landing spot yet.

steps.text: Apply to a company fitting care robots in homes and training families
Take an evening course in assistive technology and telecare
Keep the live-in work and save most of the pay
Hold off buying a home with partner Nadia until settled

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: So 2031, and robots about 2034. That's more like a plan than a panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to retrain if you start now, so start now. At work I'd organise a little session for the live-in carers on what's coming. I'd probably post the same message online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think it's a good picture for someone like me. I'd have time to get properly qualified and be a person who assesses homes for robots and telecare, rather than a carer being replaced. I'd still feel sad leaving the actual care, though.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Next year I'd start a proper part-time course in assistive technology and keep the live-in fortnights alongside it. When the AI tools land around 2031, I'd be using them from day one in my new work. I'd also put some savings into shares in companies making the care robots, which feels odd but sensible.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly okay. Uneasy about leaving people like Mrs Halloran.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the extra three years, compared with the fast one, change for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I can get qualified instead of grabbing whatever job is going. In the fast one I'd be chasing; here I'd be choosing. And Nadia and I could buy a place sooner, because I'd have a clearer path.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said investing in care robot makers feels odd. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I'd be betting on the thing that ends my old job. But I'd rather own a little bit of it than just be on the receiving end. My grandad bought shares in the company that closed his mill, and he always said it was the only smart thing he did.

I'd run a small **session for live-in carers** on what's coming.
think: I'd have time to become someone who **assesses homes** for robots and telecare.
I'd still feel **sad leaving** the actual care.

feel: **Mostly okay**, uneasy about leaving clients like Mrs Halloran.
S3.quote: My grandad bought shares in the company that closed his mill, and he always said it was the only smart thing he did.
fieldNote: The extra years let her move from **chasing to choosing**.
She'd **invest** in the companies ending her old job, as her grandad did.
Her sadness is about **the people**, not the money.

steps.text: Start a part-time assistive technology course next year
Use the new AI tools from day one around 2031
Buy shares in companies that make home care robots

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years, then robots in 2039. I'd be nearly forty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift, and anyone in care should use it. At work I'd be the annoying one telling people to start a course. Online I'd keep posting about AI for carers, like I already do a bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I'd stay in care for most of that decade, because I love it and it pays well. Then in my mid-thirties I'd want to own something, maybe a small agency that mixes live-in carers with good tech. With ten years, I could build that properly instead of rushing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing live-in work for the next few years and save hard. By thirty I'd start a small side business matching live-in carers with families, using AI for the rota and paperwork. And Nadia and I would buy a house in the next couple of years, because the timing would feel safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and a bit excited.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Your agency would be using AI for the thinking parts by 2036, and robots could do the hands-on work by 2039. Where does that leave a small care agency?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the risk, yeah. By 2039 I'd want the agency to be selling the mix, a person for company and a robot for lifting. If I've built the trust with families by then, they'd come to me for both.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do differently with ten years that you couldn't with two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Take my time and enjoy the job, honestly. With two years I'd be leaving people I love in a hurry. With ten years, I could see my client Mrs Halloran through to the end and then make my move.

I'd keep **posting about AI** for carers, as I already do.
think: I'd **stay in care** for most of the decade because I love it.
In my mid-thirties I'd want to **own a small agency** mixing carers and tech.

Start a **side business** matching live-in carers with families by thirty.

S4.quote: With ten years, I could see my client Mrs Halloran through to the end and then make my move.
fieldNote: A decade lets her **stay with clients** she loves before moving on.
Her agency plan would sell **people plus robots**, built on family trust.
She sees the risk that robots by **2039** could undercut a small agency.

steps.text: Keep doing live-in fortnights for a few years and save hard
Start a small agency matching live-in carers with families by thirty
Use AI to run the new agency's rota and paperwork

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I'd have to leave care in a rush with nowhere clear to land. What would help is someone training carers to set up and check the robots, paid for, before they arrive. Carers know the homes, so we should be the ones putting the machines in.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who checks the robot at three in the morning. That's when Mrs Halloran thinks it's a school day and needs talking down. Nobody designing care robots has ever sat with a frightened ninety-one-year-old at three in the morning.

headlineQuote: Nobody designing care robots has ever sat with a frightened ninety-one-year-old at three in the morning.
portrait: Chloe is a **27-year-old live-in carer** working fortnights with a 91-year-old woman in a village.
Good live-in pay and **over a year saved** give her real room to move.
She **uses AI daily** for logs and meal plans and would train other carers.
Fast AGI pushes her toward a **care robot company**; slower versions let her retrain properly.
With a decade she'd **build a small agency** that mixes people and tech.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, leaving care in a rush with nowhere clear to land.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid training** for carers to set up and check robots before they arrive.
